paper_metadata.title: Applying quantum autoencoders for time series anomaly detection

summary: The paper studies gate-based quantum autoencoders for time-series anomaly detection using 7 data-encoding qubits and 9 qubits during training, with ansätze including PauliTwoDesign and RealAmplitudes variants. On the simulator, the quantum models are reported to outperform a 4686-parameter classical autoencoder on the selected UCR datasets, while on IBM Torino the 21-parameter PauliTwoDesign model with quasi-amplitude encoding and 8192 shots achieves anomaly detection performance comparable to its simulated counterpart.

experiments.description: Quantum autoencoder for time series anomaly detection evaluated on IBM Qiskit statevector simulation across multiple UCR benchmark datasets, comparing reconstruction-error and Swap-Test-based anomaly classification against a classical autoencoder baseline.

algorithm.variant: Quantum autoencoder (Bravo-Prieto-style) with amplitude encoding; evaluated with reconstruction-based and Swap-Test-based anomaly detection

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each 128-point sliding window is amplitude-encoded into a 7-qubit state; during training 9 qubits are used total, with 6 latent qubits and 1 trash qubit plus ancilla/reference qubits for the Swap-Test.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize reconstruction error between input and reconstructed output, or minimize Swap-Test 1-counts for benign data; anomalies are identified by high post-processed reconstruction error or Swap-Test measurement.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Swap-Test training objective on benign data; trash qubit reset in reconstruction architecture; thresholding on post-processed metric

problem_instance.description: Time series anomaly detection on UCR Time Series Anomaly Archive benchmark datasets

dataset_specification.description: Subset of UCR anomaly datasets; each dataset has one anomaly in the test set and no anomalies in training; datasets highlighted include 28, 54, 99, 118, 138, 176

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Sliding windows of size 128 with stride 1; no normalization before state preparation; moving average postprocessing with window size 128; anomaly flagged as time step with largest post-processed value
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Average over 5 executions for each ansatz/dataset/configuration; anomaly detection rate reported; best-performing time window selected by largest post-processed value

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Sliding-window extraction; amplitude encoding; COBYLA optimization on CPU
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Mean squared error or Swap-Test measurement followed by moving average smoothing; thresholding / selecting maximum post-processed value as anomaly

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: varies by ansatz; some configurations show increasing loss with more parameters

speedup_claims.conditions: Across the tested UCR anomaly datasets on the statevector simulator
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a parameter-count reduction, not a runtime or asymptotic computational speedup.

speedup_claims.conditions: Quantum autoencoders trained for 45 epochs vs classical baseline trained for 250 epochs
speedup_claims.caveats: Reported as training-iteration reduction; no wall-clock training-time comparison is provided for the simulator experiment.

complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: 60–230x fewer trainable parameters than classical baseline; 5x fewer training iterations
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_classical: Classical autoencoder baseline has 4686 parameters and 250 epochs

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; only empirical benchmark datasets and parameter counts are reported
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Quantum autoencoders use 21-77 trainable parameters versus 4686 for the classical autoencoder; 45 training epochs versus 250 for the classical baseline
limiting_factors: Performance depends strongly on ansatz and dataset
State preparation via amplitude encoding is hardware-inefficient
Results are on a simulator, not a large-scale QPU

notes: Statevector simulator explicitly reported; 9 qubits during training and 7 qubits for data encoding are reported in the paper.
No asymptotic speedup analysis is given; only empirical parameter/epoch reductions are reported, so speedup_order is none_proven.
Authors report better anomaly detection than the classical autoencoder on the selected datasets, but this is an empirical benchmark result rather than a demonstrated practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Quantum autoencoder for time series anomaly detection executed on real IBM Torino hardware using quasi-amplitude encoding and Swap-Test-based anomaly classification, compared against a classical autoencoder baseline on the same encoded data.

algorithm.variant: Quantum autoencoder with quasi-amplitude encoding and Swap-Test-based anomaly detection on hardware
algorithm.convergence_criteria: 45 training epochs; best epoch selected by lowest loss

hyperparameters.quasi_amplitude_encoding_selection: best of 100 runs by minimum MSE

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Exact amplitude encoding was found hardware-inefficient; for hardware runs, each 128-point window is approximated by a quasi-amplitude-encoded circuit using EfficientSU2 with 7 qubits.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize Swap-Test measurement on benign data; classify anomaly when post-processed Swap-Test measurement is maximal in the valid detection range.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Swap-Test-only anomaly scoring; no reconstruction step; built-in error mitigation from Sampler

problem_instance.description: Single UCR anomaly dataset evaluated on real hardware; dataset 54 used for training and testing around the anomaly region
problem_instance.dataset_name: UCR Time Series Anomaly Archive, dataset 54

dataset_specification.description: Training data from ts=400 to 677 (150 sliding windows); test data from ts=2993 to 3363+127 including 100 windows before and 85 after the valid detection range plus the anomaly range

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Quasi-amplitude encoding generated on a classical computer using EfficientSU2 with 2 repetitions and 7 qubits; best of 100 optimization runs selected per window; Mann–Whitney U test used to compare residuals of encoded training and test data; moving average window size 30 for postprocessing
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Four executions for training-loss curves; anomaly found if a time window within the valid detection range is selected; distribution overlap between benign and anomalous post-processed measurements reported

noise_model.noise_type: NISQ hardware noise; built-in error mitigation via Sampler primitive
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: Sampler primitive with integrated error mitigation
noise_model.mitigation_details: Sampler primitive used; 8192 shots chosen as maximum available on IBM Torino at the time of writing

implementation_details.framework_version: Qiskit (version not fully specified); IBM Sampler primitive
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Quasi-amplitude encoding via EfficientSU2 on a classical computer; best of 100 runs selected per window; classical optimization with SPSA for quasi-encoding circuit
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Swap-Test measurements smoothed with moving average window 30; anomaly selected by largest post-processed value in valid detection range; distribution overlap analysis
implementation_details.total_execution_time: Approximately 8.25h per experiment; 21h total quantum computing time across experiments
implementation_details.quantum_execution_time: Approximately 5.25h quantum computing time per experiment; about 7 min per epoch and 11 min per epoch wall time reported

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: simulator converges faster; hardware shows more gradual decline with fewer erratic spikes

speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic or empirical speedup is claimed; the paper reports comparable anomaly detection performance on hardware and simulator, but with substantial quantum runtime cost.

complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: Quantum autoencoder on hardware matched simulated anomaly detection performance; no asymptotic speedup claimed
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_classical: Classical autoencoder failed to correctly identify the anomaly on this dataset
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: Approximately 8.25h per experiment on IBM Torino

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not established; single dataset (54) and small-scale 9-qubit hardware run
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Quantum autoencoder on IBM Torino with 21 trainable parameters and 8192 shots; classical baseline is evaluated on the same quasi-amplitude-encoded data
limiting_factors: Quasi-amplitude encoding is a workaround for exact amplitude encoding inefficiency
No scaling study beyond a single dataset and small qubit count
Comparison is against a baseline on encoded data, not a full end-to-end practical deployment

notes: IBM Torino hardware explicitly reported; quasi-amplitude encoding and EfficientSU2 with 7 qubits are explicitly described.
No circuit depth or transpiled depth values are given in the paper, so those fields remain null.
No asymptotic complexity or speedup order is stated; only empirical performance and runtime are reported.

The paper states the quantum autoencoder on real hardware matches the anomaly detection performance of its simulated counterpart, but does not establish a clear practical advantage over classical methods.
